Operation and Maintenance Manuals for Electrical Systems

1. Introduction Purpose of the Manual

This manual provides detailed operational and maintenance instructions for Low Tension (LT) Panels, Distribution Boards (DB), Power Points (sockets), Cable Trays, and Wiring systems in a building or facility. It is intended to ensure proper use, safety, and longevity of the system components.

Overview of the Electrical System

The electrical system distributes power from the main source to various parts of the building, enabling the operation of equipment and devices. The LT panel is the primary distribution point, feeding power to distribution boards (DB) that distribute it further to power points and other devices via wiring and cable trays.

2. System Components LT Panels

  • Function: The LT panel receives electricity from the transformer or generator and distributes it to DBs and other loads in the building.
  • Components: Circuit breakers, isolators, busbars, relays, meters, and protection devices.

Distribution Boards (DB)

  • Function: A distribution board splits the electrical power supply into subsidiary circuits while providing a fuse or circuit breaker for each circuit.
  • Components: MCBs (Miniature Circuit Breakers), MCCBs (Molded Case Circuit Breakers), RCDs (Residual Current Devices), and neutral links.

Power Points (Sockets)

  • Function: Power points or sockets provide direct electrical connections for equipment and appliances. They can be single-phase or three-phase depending on the application.
  • Components: Sockets, switches, and protective covers.

Cable Trays

  • Function: Cable trays support and protect electrical cables, facilitating neat and organized cable routing.
  • Components: Perforated trays, ladder trays, bends, and junctions.

Wiring

  • Function: Wiring connects all electrical components, distributing power safely and efficiently across the building.
  • Types: PVC-insulated copper cables, armored cables for high-power applications, and control cables.

3. Operation of Electrical Systems LT Panels Operation

Pre-Start Inspection:

  • Ensure all breakers and isolators are in the off position before powering the panel.

Switching On:

  • Turn on the main isolator to power the system.
  • Sequentially switch on individual breakers for different circuits to avoid overloading.
  • Check meters for voltage, current, and power factor readings to ensure normal operation.

Normal Operation:

  • Monitor for any alarms or unusual readings (such as overcurrent or low voltage).
  • Ensure cooling fans (if installed) are operating efficiently to avoid overheating.
  • Perform regular inspections of the busbar and wiring insulation for signs of wear or damage.

Shutdown Procedure:

  • Switch off all breakers sequentially before turning off the main isolator.
  • Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) procedures should be followed during maintenance.

DB Operation

Circuit Breaker Management:

  • Always switch off the circuit breaker before working on any connected circuit or device.
  • Ensure that the correct breaker rating is used for the associated load.

Residual Current Devices (RCDs):

  • RCDs should be tested regularly using the test button to ensure functionality.
  • If an RCD trips frequently, check for faulty appliances or wiring.

Power Points (Sockets) Operation Pre-Use Check:

  • Inspect for damage such as loose connections or cracks in the casing.
  • Ensure proper earthing and that the socket is connected to the correct phase.

In-Use Safety:

  • Avoid overloading sockets with too many devices, especially high-current appliances like heaters or motors.
  • Use sockets designed for the required voltage and current rating of the connected equipment.

Cable Tray and Wiring Guidelines Installation:

  • Securely mount cable trays along designated routes with proper support spacing.
  • Cables should be neatly arranged within the tray without crossing or tangling.

Cable Management:

  • Ensure cables are properly insulated and clamped to avoid damage from vibrations.
  • Avoid overloading trays with too many cables, which can cause heat buildup.

Wiring Operation:

  • Use appropriately sized cables based on load requirements and run length.
  • Periodically inspect cables for insulation damage, particularly in high- stress areas such as bends and junctions

4. Maintenance Procedures Routine Maintenance

LT Panels:

  • LT Panels : Inspect for dust accumulation, check for loose connections, and clean the panel exterior.
  • DB : Inspect for signs of overheating or corrosion, clean dust from breakers.
  • Power Point :Visually inspect sockets for wear or damage, check the tightness of wiring.
  • Cable Tray : Check for proper support of the trays and any signs of corrosion.
  • Wiring : Inspect exposed wiring for cuts, nicks, or abrasions
  • For Six Months : Refer Six months Maintenance Checklist for Electrical
  • For Annually : Refer Yearly Maintenance Checklist for Electrical

Troubleshooting and Repairs Circuit Breaker Tripping:

  • Cause: Overload, short circuit, or faulty breaker.
  • Solution: Identify the overloaded circuit and redistribute the load or replace the faulty breaker.

Power Outages:

  • Cause: Loose connections, blown fuses, or main power failure.
  • Solution: Check wiring and connections, replace fuses, and ensure there are no supply issues.

Voltage Fluctuations:

  • Cause: Unbalanced loads or poor quality power supply.
  • Solution: Check load distribution and stabilize the system using voltage stabilizers or proper load balancing techniques.

5. Safety Guidelines Electrical Safety Precautions

  • De-energize Before Maintenance: Always disconnect the power supply before performing any maintenance or repairs.
  • Lockout/Tagout (LOTO): Use lockout/tagout procedures to ensure that equipment remains powered off during service.
  • Avoid Water: Never operate electrical equipment in wet conditions, and ensure that all devices are properly waterproofed if in a moisture-prone area.

Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)

  • Gloves: Use insulated gloves when working on live equipment.
  • Safety Glasses: Wear eye protection to guard against arc flashes or debris.
  • Insulated Footwear: Use non-conductive footwear when working near electrical equipment.

Emergency Shutdown Procedures

  • In case of an electrical emergency (such as a fire or shock), immediately shut off the main power supply at the LT panel.
  • Use only non-conductive equipment to address electrical fires (e.g., Class C fire extinguishers).
  • Follow the facility's emergency response plan.

7. Recommended Spare Parts

  • Circuit breakers
  • Fuses
  • Busbar connectors
  • Socket outlets
  • Cable clamps
  • RCDs/ELCBs

8. Warranty Information

Refer Warranty Certificate from Nirmaan for details.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Operations and Maintenance (O&M) Manual is intended to provide comprehensive information for the safe and efficient operation, maintenance, and troubleshooting of the Electrical Panel installed at the project site. The manual ensures reliability, safety, and long- term performance of the system, and is intended for use by operation and facility maintenance personnel.

This document includes technical specifications, operational guidelines, maintenance procedures, and safety protocols in accordance with the relevant Indian and international standards (IEC, IS, IEEE).

2. PANEL OVERVIEW

ParameterDescription
Panel TypeMain LT Panel / Distribution Panel / HVAC Panel / Fire Panel
Rated Voltage415V, 3 Phase, 4 Wire, 50 Hz
Short Circuit Rating25 - 50kA for 1 Sec
Panel ConstructionCompartmentalized, Powder-Coated CRCA Sheet, IP54 Rating
Control DevicesIndication Lamps, Selector Switches, Digital Meters
Protection DevicesMCCBs, MCBs, ELCBs, SPD, Earth Fault Relay

3. SAFETY INSTRUCTIONS

  • All operation and maintenance shall be carried out only by qualified personnel.
  • Ensure the electrical supply is isolated before opening or servicing the panel.
  • Wear PPE including arc flash suit, insulated gloves, safety glasses, and antistatic shoes.
  • Use lockout-tagout (LOTO) procedures before any service.
  • Keep a CO2 or ABC fire extinguisher nearby.
  • Avoid water or cleaning liquids near live circuits.
  • Follow all IS/IEC safety norms applicable to LV panels.

4. OPERATION PROCEDURE

4.1 Panel Start-Up

  • Inspect panel externally and internally for any physical damage.
  • Verify that all terminals and cables are securely fastened.
  • Ensure all outgoing breakers are in OFF condition.
  • Switch ON the main incoming ACB/MCCB.
  • Sequentially turn ON outgoing feeders as per operational priority.
  • Check phase indication, voltage, and current readings on meters.

4.2 Panel Shutdown

  • Switch OFF all outgoing breakers one by one.
  • Switch OFF the main incoming breaker.
  • Isolate supply at the upstream source.
  • Apply LOTO tags and padlocks if maintenance is to be performed.

4.3 Normal Operation

  • Ensure all breakers are operating within rated parameters.
  • Monitor current load regularly and avoid overloading.
  • Check phase indicators and meter readings daily.
  • Maintain ambient temperature within 0-40°C.
  • Ensure the panel area is dry, clean, and ventilated.

5. MAINTENANCE PROCEDURES

5.1 Preventive Maintenance Schedule

5.2 Cleaning Procedure

Breaker Mechanical OperationQuarterlyOperate all breakers manually to prevent jamming
Retightening TerminalsHalf-YearlyCheck and torque all power and control terminals
IR TestingYearlyMegger test phase to phase and phase to earth
ThermographyYearlyIdentify abnormal heating or hotspots
Meter CalibrationYearlyEnsure energy meters and ammeters are accurate
Protection Relay TestingYearlyTest under simulated fault conditions
  • De-energize panel using LOTO procedure.
  • Remove dust and dirt using a vacuum cleaner or dry cloth.
  • Use a blower to remove dust from internal components.
  • Check for rust or corrosion and apply anti-rust treatment if necessary

Unusual noiseLoose connection, arcingShut down panel and investigate immediately
Panel overheatingOverloaded circuit, loose terminalsPerform thermography, balance load, tighten lugs
Lights flickeringLoose terminal or voltage fluctuationCheck cable terminations, measure voltage stability

1. Introduction

1.1 Purpose

This manual provides detailed instructions for the operation and maintenance of the Direct Expansion (DX) HVAC system. It is intended for use by facility operators, maintenance personnel, and service technicians to ensure efficient and safe operation.

1.2 Scope

The DX HVAC system is designed to provide cooling, heating, and ventilation for commercial and industrial applications. This manual covers the operation, preventive maintenance, troubleshooting, and safety requirements of the system.

2. System Overview

2.1 System Description

The DX HVAC system consists of the following major components:

  • Compressor: Circulates refrigerant in the system.
  • Condenser Coil: Releases heat absorbed by the refrigerant.
  • Evaporator Coil: Absorbs heat from the air and provides cooling.
  • Expansion Valve: Regulates the flow of refrigerant.
  • Air Handling Unit (AHU): Distributes conditioned air into the space.
  • Control Panel: Includes thermostats, sensors, and switches for system operation.

3. Operating Instructions

3.1 Pre-Operation Checks

  • Ensure the power supply matches the system requirements.
  • Inspect the air filters, refrigerant lines, and electrical connections.
  • Verify that the thermostat settings are appropriate
  • Ensure no obstructions block the airflow around the outdoor and indoor units.

3.2 Startup Procedure

  • Switch on the main power supply.
  • Set the thermostat to the desired temperature.
  • Monitor the system for normal operation:
    • Compressor starts without delay.
    • No unusual noise or vibration.
    • Proper airflow from supply vents.

3.3 Normal Operation

  • Maintain consistent thermostat settings to prevent frequent cycling.
  • Monitor system indicators for temperature, pressure, and operational status.
  • Avoid tampering with system controls during operation.

3.4 Shutdown Procedure

  • Set the thermostat to the "Off" position.
  • Turn off the main power supply.
  • Perform a visual inspection for any signs of wear or damage.

4. Maintenance Schedule

  • Inspect for unusual noise, leaks, or vibrations.
  • Check system indicators for temperature and pressure readings.
  • Inspect refrigerant lines and connections for leaks or damage.
  • Verify thermostat and sensor accuracy.

5. Troubleshooting Guide

IssuePossible CauseSolution
System not coolingLow refrigerant levelsCheck and refill refrigerant.
Compressor not startingElectrical faultInspect and repair connections.
Ice formation on coilsDirty filters or low refrigerantClean filters and inspect.
Unusual noise or vibrationLoose parts or compressor faultTighten parts or replace.
High energy consumptionDirty coils or filtersClean coils and replace filters.

6. Safety Instructions

  • Disconnect power supply before performing maintenance.
  • Use appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) during servicing.
  • Follow EPA regulations for refrigerant handling and disposal.
  • Do not operate the system without proper grounding.
  • Keep the area around the outdoor unit clear of debris and obstructions.

This manual outlines the operation and maintenance guidelines for the chilled water piping system and cassette units installed within the HVAC system. Proper operation and maintenance are critical for ensuring optimal performance, energy efficiency, and system longevity.

The following are the key components of an O&M manual for Chilled Water systems:

1. System Overview:

The chilled water piping system distributes cooled water from the chiller to air handling units (AHUs) and cassette units. This water absorbs heat from the building spaces and returns to the chiller to be cooled again. The piping is typically insulated to prevent heat gain and condensation. Cassette units are ceiling-mounted HVAC devices designed to deliver cooled or heated air efficiently. They utilize the chilled water from the piping system to cool indoor spaces. The fan in the cassette unit circulates room air across cooling coils, which absorb heat from the air.

2. System Operation:

  • Chilled water flows through insulated pipes from the chiller to the cassette units. The flow is controlled by motorized or manual valves at various points in the system.
  • The chilled water temperature is typically maintained between 4°C and 10°C (39°F to 50°F) by the chiller or as required by the client.
  • Proper pressure must be maintained throughout the system. This is ensured by the pumps that circulate the water.
  • The fan inside the cassette unit pulls warm air from the room and passes it over the chilled water coils.
  • Heat is absorbed by the chilled water, and cooled air is blown back into the room.
  • The thermostat connected to the unit adjusts the flow of chilled water to regulate room temperature.
  • The fan speed can be adjusted (low, medium, high) to control air circulation and cooling intensity.

3. Routine Maintenance Procedure:

  • Conduct regular inspections for leaks, especially at joints, valves, and connections.
  • Ensure that the pipe insulation is intact and free from damage to prevent energy loss and condensation.
  • Test the water for proper chemical balance (pH, anti-corrosion agents) to prevent corrosion, scaling, and biological growth.
  • Monitor the flow rate of chilled water to ensure it meets the system's design parameters.
  • Periodically perform pressure tests to check for weaknesses or leaks in the piping system.
  • Clean or replace the filters every 2-3 months to maintain proper airflow and air quality.
  • Clean the evaporator coils to prevent dirt buildup, which can reduce cooling efficiency.
  • Ensure that the thermostat is functioning properly and set to the desired temperature.
  • Inspect and lubricate fan motors and bearings to avoid mechanical failure and ensure efficient operation.
  • Regularly check and clean the condensate drain to avoid clogging and water leakage.
  • Periodically check for any unusual noise, vibrations, or damage to the cassette unit.

4. Troubleshooting Guidelines

IssuePossible CauseSolution
No cooling from the cassette unitThermostat malfunctionCheck and reset the thermostat settings
Insufficient chilled water flowVerify pump operation and check flow rates
Blocked air filtersClean or replace the filters
Water leakage from the unitBlocked condensate drainClean the condensate drain
Improper pipe insulationInspect and replace damaged insulation
Low cooling efficiencyDirty coilsClean evaporator coils
Incorrect chilled water temperatureCheck chiller settings and water temperature
High water pressure in the pipingValve malfunctionInspect and adjust the valves
Pump speed too highReduce pump speed to match system requirements

5. Safety Precautions

  • Always disconnect the power supply before servicing any electrical components.
  • Ensure proper drainage when inspecting or cleaning the condensate system to avoid water spills and damage.
  • Wear appropriate PPE such as gloves, safety glasses, and protective clothing when working with chilled water or refrigerants.
  • Handle water treatment chemicals with care, and follow the manufacturer's guidelines for usage.

Operation and Maintenance Manuals for Air Handling Unit

1. Introduction

This manual provides detailed instructions for the operation, maintenance, and servicing of the Chilled water system Air Handling Unit (AHU). Proper operation and maintenance of this system are essential for ensuring efficient cooling, air circulation, and air filtration in the environment where it is installed.

The chilled water AHU is designed to cool and dehumidify the air that passes through the system, using chilled water as the cooling medium. The unit also includes filtration and air circulation components to maintain indoor air quality (IAQ).

2. System Overview

Basic Working Principle of Chilled Water System AHU

The AHU draws in return air from the conditioned space and mixes it with fresh air. This mixed air then passes through filters, where dust and particulates are removed. The chilled water coil cools the air by absorbing heat, lowering its temperature, and reducing humidity before the fans distribute it back into the conditioned space.

Components of the AHU

  • Chilled Water Coil: The core component that cools the air passing through the unit by transferring heat from the air to the chilled water circulating through the coil.
  • Fans and Blowers: The centrifugal fan circulates air through the unit. It can be belt-driven or directly coupled to the motor.
  • Filters: The AHU is equipped with primary and secondary filters that trap dust and particulates to ensure clean air circulation.
  • Dampers: Dampers control the intake of fresh air, re-circulation of return air, and exhaust air discharge.
  • Control Valves: Modulating control valves regulate the flow of chilled water through the coil.
  • Sensors: Temperature, humidity, and pressure sensors monitor the operation and provide feedback to the control system for optimal performance.

3. Operating Procedures

Pre-Start Inspection

  • Check all electrical connections for tightness.
  • Ensure that the chilled water supply is adequate and the valves are in the correct position.
  • Inspect filters for cleanliness.
  • Ensure that the fans, blowers, and other mechanical components are free from obstructions.

Startup Procedure

  • Open the chilled water supply and return valves.
  • Power on the control system.
  • Set the desired temperature on the thermostat.
  • Gradually start the fans and blowers using the VFD. Increase the speed as required.
  • Monitor the inlet and outlet temperatures of the chilled water coil to ensure cooling is occurring.
  • Observe the air pressure drop across the filters.

Normal Operation

  • The system will automatically maintain the desired temperature using the control valves and VFD to regulate airflow and cooling capacity.
  • Ensure continuous monitoring of the temperature, humidity, and pressure readings on the control panel.
  • Inspect filters and replace or clean as necessary.

Shut Down Procedure

  • Gradually reduce the fan speed using the VFD.
  • Close the chilled water supply and return valves.
  • Turn off the electrical supply to the AHU.
  • Perform a post-shutdown inspection of filters, coils, and fans.

4. Control System and Settings

  • Thermostats: Maintain the room temperature by modulating the chilled water flow.
  • Control Valves: Regulate the chilled water entering the cooling coil, controlled by the thermostat.
  • Pressure and Temperature Set Points:
    • Chilled Water Inlet Temperature: Typically 7°C (adjustable as required)
    • Chilled Water Outlet Temperature: Typically 12°C
  • Variable Frequency Drives (VFD): Used for fan speed control to optimize energy use and achieve variable air volume (VAV) flow rates.

5. Routine Maintenance

Daily Inspection

  • Check the overall performance of the unit, ensuring that the temperature and humidity levels are within the set range.
  • Ensure no unusual noise or vibration from the fan or motor.

Monthly Preventive Maintenance

  • Inspect and clean the filters.
  • Check the condition of the fan belts and pulleys. Tighten or replace as necessary.
  • Inspect the cooling coil for any blockages or dirt accumulation.

Quarterly and Annual Maintenance

  • Clean the chilled water coils using appropriate coil cleaner.
  • Lubricate the fan bearings and inspect for wear.
  • Inspect the motor electrical connections.
  • Test the operation of dampers and actuators.
  • Replace filters if necessary.
  • Conduct an overall system performance check to ensure all components are functioning optimally.

6. Troubleshooting

Common Issues and Solutions

Poor Cooling Performance:

  • Check if the chilled water supply is sufficient.
  • Inspect the coil for dirt or blockages.
  • Verify control valve operation.

Excessive Noise or Vibration:

  • Inspect fan bearings and belts.
  • Check if the fan is out of balance.

High Air Pressure Drop:

  • Clean or replace dirty filters.
  • Inspect the airflow passages for obstructions.

System Not Responding to Controls:

  • Check the control panel for any fault codes.
  • Reset the control system if necessary.

7. Safety Guidelines

  • Always wear appropriate Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), including gloves, safety goggles, and hearing protection when working on the unit.
  • Follow all electrical safety procedures when performing maintenance on the control panel or electrical components.
  • Handle refrigerants and other chemicals in accordance with environmental and safety regulations.
  • In the event of an emergency, immediately shut down the system by using the emergency stop button located on the control panel.

1. Introduction

This manual provides detailed instructions for the operation, maintenance, and servicing of the Air Washer Unit. Proper operation and maintenance are critical for ensuring the effective performance of the system in cooling and air filtration, improving indoor air quality in industrial, commercial, and residential settings.

The air washer system utilizes evaporation cooling principles, cooling and humidifying the air while simultaneously removing airborne contaminants such as dust and particulate matter. This system is commonly used in environments where humidity control and air cleanliness are priorities.

2. System Overview

Basic Working Principle of an Air Washer Unit

The air washer works by drawing in hot, dry air and passing it through water-saturated cooling pads, where the water evaporates, reducing the temperature of the air. As the air passes through these pads, dust and particulate matter are also washed out, improving air quality. The cooled and cleaned air is then blown into the space via fans or blowers.

Components of the Air Washer Unit

  • Airflow System: Comprises of inlet and outlet ducts for air intake and distribution. Air is drawn in and forced through the cooling pads by the blower.
  • Water Distribution System: Includes a pump, water distribution pipes, and nozzles to evenly distribute water over the cooling pads.
  • Evaporative Cooling Pads: High-efficiency pads that are saturated with water to allow heat exchange, reducing air temperature as air passes through them.
  • Blowers and Fans: These drive air through the unit and the cooling pads into the conditioned space. They can be belt-driven or directly coupled to the motor.
  • Filters: Pre-filters are used to trap larger dust particles before the air reaches the cooling pads.
  • Control Panel: Includes switches, temperature and humidity controls, and system status indicators.

3. Operating Procedures

Pre-Start Inspection

  • Check the unit for any visible damage, including the water distribution system and pads.
  • Ensure that all electrical connections are tight and secure.
  • Verify that water levels in the storage tank are adequate, and the pump is operational.
  • Inspect filters to ensure they are clean and free from obstructions.
  • Ensure the blower motor and fan belts are in good condition and properly tensioned.

Startup Procedure

  • Switch on the control panel.
  • Turn on the water pump to start water circulation in the cooling pads.
  • Set the desired fan speed using the VFD (if available).
  • Set the desired temperature and humidity level on the control system.
  • Gradually start the fan/blower to circulate air through the unit.
  • Monitor the unit for the first few minutes to ensure that the cooling pads are uniformly wet and the air temperature is dropping.

Normal Operation

  • The system will continuously draw air, pass it through the cooling pads, and distribute it into the space.
  • Periodically check the water level, air temperature, and pressure drop across the filters.
  • Ensure the cooling pads remain saturated and clean to maintain performance.

Shutdown Procedure

  • Gradually reduce the fan speed before turning it off.
  • Turn off the water pump after ensuring that water has drained from the pads.
  • Power off the control panel and disconnect the unit from the main power supply.
  • Inspect the unit after shutdown for any potential issues or dirt buildup.

4. Control System and Settings

  • Airflow Control: Airflow is typically controlled through the fan speed, which can be adjusted via a VFD. Lower speeds may be used during mild conditions, while higher speeds are required during peak cooling demands.
  • Water Flow Adjustment: The water flow rate can be adjusted based on the ambient air temperature and humidity. High temperatures will require more water flow to achieve effective cooling.
  • Temperature and Humidity Settings: These can be set using the control panel. The system will automatically adjust water and airflow to maintain the desired indoor temperature and humidity.

5. Routine Maintenance

Daily Inspection

  • Ensure that the water distribution system is functioning correctly and that the cooling pads are uniformly wet.
  • Check for any unusual noises from the blower or motor.
  • Verify that the water level is within acceptable limits and there are no leaks.

Monthly Preventive Maintenance

  • Clean the filters to remove dust and debris.
  • Inspect the cooling pads for dirt or scale buildup. Clean or replace as necessary.
  • Check fan belts for wear and adjust tension as needed.
  • Lubricate the blower motor bearings according to manufacturer recommendations.

Quarterly and Annual Maintenance

  • Conduct a thorough cleaning of the cooling pads, and descale if necessary.
  • Inspect the entire water distribution system for blockages or damage.
  • Test all sensors and control systems for accurate performance.
  • Inspect electrical connections and ensure the motor is running efficiently.

6. Troubleshooting

Common Issues and Solutions

Inadequate Cooling:

  • Check if the cooling pads are properly wetted.
  • Ensure the fan is running at the appropriate speed.
  • Clean or replace clogged filters.

Excessive Noise from the Unit:

  • Inspect fan belts and motor bearings for wear.
  • Tighten any loose components.

Water Leaks:

  • Check for damaged pipes or fittings in the water distribution system.

System Not Responding to Controls:

  • Verify power supply and reset the control panel if necessary.
  • Inspect control wiring for damage or loose connections.

7. Safety Guidelines

  • Always wear appropriate Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), including gloves, safety goggles, and hearing protection when servicing the unit.
  • Follow electrical safety protocols and ensure the unit is de-energized before performing maintenance.
  • Be cautious when working with the water system to prevent slips or falls due to wet surfaces.
  • In case of emergency, use the emergency stop button located on the control panel to shut down the unit immediately.

8. Service and Spare Parts

Recommended Spare Parts List

  • Cooling pads
  • Filters
  • Fan belts
  • Water pump
  • Sensors and control relays

This manual provides detailed instructions for the operation, maintenance, and troubleshooting of Variable Refrigerant Flow (VRF) systems in accordance with ASHRAE standards. Proper adherence to these guidelines ensures optimal performance, energy efficiency, and system longevity.

  • Refrigerant Piping: Insulated piping network for refrigerant circulation.
  • Control Systems: Centralized and localized controllers for operation management.

3.3 Shut-Down

  • Deactivate the outdoor unit from the main control system.
  • Isolate the power supply if the system will remain idle for an extended period.

  • Shut down the system immediately if abnormal sounds, odors, or smoke are detected.
  • Isolate the electrical supply.
  • Contact authorized service personnel for repairs.

6.1 Refrigerant Handling

  • Use certified technicians for refrigerant charging and recovery
  • Avoid venting refrigerants into the atmosphere; comply with local environmental regulations.

2.1 Description of CCTV System

  • Monitors: For real-time viewing and playback.

  • Network Components: Routers, switches, and network cables for IP-based systems.
  • Storage Devices: Hard drives or cloud storage for video archives.
  • Accessories: Mounting brackets, enclosures, and surge protectors.

2.2 System Features

  • Continuous or motion-triggered recording
  • Remote access and control via mobile apps or web interfaces.
  • High-definition video resolution (up to 4K).
  • Infrared (IR) or low-light capability for night surveillance.
  • Analytic features like motion detection, face recognition, and license plate recognition.

1.Introduction

The Access Control System (ACS) is an integral part of a building's security infrastructure. It restricts or permits access to doors based on credential verification. The system typically comprises an access control panel, controllers, door readers (biometric, card, and/or PIN), electromagnetic locks, and door release mechanisms like push buttons.

This manual provides comprehensive guidelines for the operation, safe handling, installation and maintenance practices for a generic Access Control System.

2.System Overview

System Components

ComponentDescription
Access Control PanelCentral hub that interfaces with the Building Management System or Server. Manages access rules, logs, and event data.
4-Door ControllerControls access for up to 4 doors. Interfaces with readers, EM locks, door contacts, and exit buttons.
Readers (Biometric/Card/PIN)Devices mounted at entry points to authenticate credentials.
Push Button (Exit)Allows for manual door release, typically from inside the secured area.
Electromagnetic (EM) LockHigh-strength door lock that secures doors electromagnetically. Operates fail-safe (unlocks on power loss).
Power Supply UnitSupplies regulated power (typically 12VDC or 24VDC) to the system components.

3.Installation Guidelines

WARNING: Only trained and certified personnel should carry out installation. Ensure power is OFF during wiring.

3.1.General Installation Principles

  • Always follow low-voltage wiring regulations.
  • Use shielded twisted pair for communication lines.
  • Avoid routing cables near power lines or electrical equipment to reduce interference.
  • All wiring should be labeled, terminated in proper enclosures, and protected from mechanical damage.

3.2.Access Control Panel

  • Mounting Location: Secure, ventilated, dry area such as a communication room or electrical shaft.
  • Enclosure: Use tamper-resistant, lockable enclosures.
  • Connections: Connect to network (LAN), power supply, and controller interface.
  • Power: Dedicated power circuit with surge protection is recommended.

3.3. 4-Door Controller

Mounting: Wall-mounted near the doors it controls.

Cabling:

  • Readers: 6/8-core shielded cable.
  • EM Locks: 2-core 1.5mm² cable.
  • Push Button: 2-core cable.
  • Door Contact: 2-core cable.

Power Backup: Should be connected to UPS or battery backup.

3.4. Readers

Mounting Height:

  • Card/PIN Reader: 1200 mm from floor level.
  • Biometric: 1350 mm for ergonomic use.
  • Mounting Surface: Must be flat, near the door (secured side).
  • Wiring Distance: Max recommended distance from controller is 100 meters.
  • Weather Protection: Use IP-rated readers or weatherproof enclosures for outdoor use.

3.5. Push Button

  • Location: 1200 mm AFFL on the non-secured side.
  • Type: Should be “No-touch” IR sensor type or press-type as per client requirement.
  • Emergency Provision: Should be connected in parallel with emergency break glass unit (where applicable).

3.6. Electromagnetic Locks

  • Mounting: On the top frame of the door and armature plate on the door leaf.
  • Alignment: Ensure perfect alignment between the lock and the armature plate.
  • Fixing Hardware: Use through bolts for armature plate and mounting brackets for locks.
  • Power Wiring: Use 2-core cable with ferrite beads if EMI is expected.

4. System Operation

4.1.Access Control Panel

  • Manages users, credentials, and access rules.
  • Logs events such as successful entries, denied access, forced entry, etc.
  • Interfaces with Fire Alarm Panel for fail-safe unlock during emergency.

4.2. 4-Door Controller

  • Receives inputs from readers and grants or denies access.
  • Outputs to EM locks and logs door events.
  • Monitors door status (open/closed) using door sensors.

4.3. Readers

  • Biometric Readers: Use fingerprint/face scan to authenticate.
  • Card Readers: Validate proximity or smart cards (13.56 MHz or 125 KHz).
  • PIN Readers: Require input of user-defined codes.
  • Readers signal the controller upon credential presentation.

4.4.Push Button

  • Sends signal to controller to momentarily release the door lock.
  • Some versions may directly interrupt EM lock power (fail-safe design).

4.5.Electromagnetic Lock

  • Remains locked when energized; unlocks when power is removed.
  • Controlled via relay output from controller or manual button.
  • Integrates with fire alarm system for auto-release during emergency.

5.Operational Procedures

5.1.User Enrollment

  • Done via access control software or locally at controller.
  • Assign access levels (door permissions, time zones).
  • Biometric data should be enrolled with quality check.

5.2. Granting Access

  • Users must present valid credential at the reader.
  • Reader sends data to controller for authentication.
  • If verified, controller unlocks EM lock momentarily.
  • Access event is logged centrally.

5.3. Exit Operation

  • Exit push button activates release circuit.
  • Door opens upon pressing the button.
  • System may log exit if door contact is present.

5.4. Emergency Release

  • Fire Alarm Trigger: All EM locks auto-release.
  • Emergency Break Glass: Break to cut lock power manually.
  • Fail-Safe Design: Locks release upon power failure.

6.Troubleshooting Guide

SymptomPossible CauseRemedy
Door not unlockingInvalid credential / Power issueVerify card/biometric. Check power supply & wiring.
EM Lock always openController output faulty / Door unlockedCheck controller relay. Inspect settings.
Reader not respondingNo power / Cable issueCheck supply voltage. Recheck cable terminations.
Biometric not acceptingDirty sensor / Low quality scanClean sensor. Re-enroll user with correct method.
Push button not workingCable disconnection / Faulty buttonCheck cable continuity and button contact.

7.Safety Cautions & Warnings

WARNING: Improper installation can result in malfunction, electric shock, or security compromise.

Cautions

  • Do not exceed maximum current ratings of EM locks or readers.
  • Always use cable ferrules and shielded cables to avoid interference.
  • Provide strain relief to all field cables at the controller.
  • Ground the controller and metal parts to avoid electrostatic interference.

Warnings

  • Do NOT connect EM locks directly to high-voltage sources.
  • Avoid exposing biometric readers to direct sunlight or water unless rated IP65/IP67.
  • Reader tampering or controller access by unauthorized persons may compromise system integrity.
  • Ensure integration with fire alarm is properly tested. Locks must release on fire signal.

8. Decommissioning Procedure

  • Remove all users and disable access from software.
  • Power down controller and panel.
  • Label and isolate wiring for future re-use if applicable.
  • Physically remove readers, locks, and buttons with minimal damage to surfaces.

9.Conclusion

This manual serves as a universal operational guide for typical access control systems deployed in commercial office environments. It ensures safe and efficient use of hardware while keeping the system reliable and secure. Periodic audits and system checks (though not covered in this manual) are recommended for optimal performance.

Overview of Fire Alarm System

The fire alarm system is designed to detect fire hazards, raise alarms, and trigger evacuation procedures. It comprises smoke/heat detectors, manual call points, sounders, strobe lights, and a central control panel, all of which work together to detect, notify, and respond to potential fire hazards.

2. System Components

Control Panel

  • Function: The central hub of the fire alarm system, the control panel monitors inputs from detectors and manual call points, activates notification devices, and provides real-time status information.
  • Components: LCD/LED display, control keys (reset, silence, evacuate, etc.), internal circuitry for monitoring and control.

Detectors

  • Smoke Detectors: Detect smoke particles in the air, signaling the control panel in case of fire.
  • Heat Detectors: Trigger alarms when they sense a rapid increase in temperature or when the temperature exceeds a pre-set threshold.
  • Multi-Sensor Detectors: Combine smoke and heat detection for greater accuracy.

Manual Call Points (MCP)

  • Function: Allow occupants to manually trigger the fire alarm by breaking the glass and pressing the button in case they spot a fire.
  • Placement: Usually located near exits or in high-traffic areas for easy access during emergencies.

Notification Devices

  • Sounders/Hooters: Audible alarms that alert building occupants to evacuate.
  • Strobes/Visual Alarms: Flashing lights designed to alert hearing-impaired occupants or those in noisy environments.

Auxiliary Devices

  • Relays: Used to interface with external systems such as building management systems (BMS), emergency lighting, or sprinkler systems.
  • Power Supplies: Includes battery backup systems to ensure continuous operation during power outages.

3. Operation of Fire Alarm System

Control Panel Operations

Normal Mode:

  • The control panel continuously monitors the detectors and displays the status (normal, alarm, or fault conditions).
  • The system will remain in a "ready" state unless a fire or fault is detected.

Fire Alarm Mode:

  • Upon detection of a fire by detectors or activation of a manual call point, the control panel enters alarm mode.
  • Sounders, sirens, and strobes are activated, and the fire event is logged on the control panel.
  • The location of the triggered device is displayed for immediate response.

Silence Alarms:

  • Authorized personnel can silence the audible alarms via the control panel to prevent unnecessary disruption after verifying the fire is under control.
  • This does not reset the system, which remains in the alarm state until reset.

Reset System:

  • After an alarm event has been resolved, the system must be reset by pressing the reset button on the control panel.
  • The reset procedure clears any previous alarm or fault conditions and returns the system to normal monitoring mode.

Fault Conditions:

  • The control panel indicates faults such as wiring issues, battery failures, or malfunctioning detectors.
  • Fault conditions require immediate investigation and resolution.

Fire Detection and Notification

  • Automatic Detection: Smoke or heat detectors automatically detect fire and trigger alarms.
  • Manual Activation: MCPs allow manual initiation of the alarm if occupants spot a fire before automatic detection. Press the MCP to trigger an immediate alarm and notify all building occupants to evacuate.

System Reset

  • After confirming the absence of fire or once the fire has been extinguished, reset the system by:
  • Checking the control panel for the alarm's source.
  • Pressing the system reset button on the panel.

4. Maintenance Procedures

Routine Inspection and Testing

Daily:

  • Check control panel for any fault or alarm indications.
  • Ensure that the system is in normal operation mode.

Weekly:

  • Test one manual call point and one detector (a different one each week) to confirm the alarm sounds and the control panel indicates the correct location.
  • Visually inspect detectors and MCPs for damage or obstructions.

Monthly:

  • Refer Six months Maintenance Checklist for Fire Alarm System

Annually:

  • Refer Yearly Maintenance Checklist for Fire Alarm System

Fault Diagnosis and Troubleshooting

No Power to Control Panel:

  • Cause: Loss of power or battery failure.
  • Solution: Check main power supply and verify the backup battery status.

Detector Malfunction:

  • Cause: Dirty or faulty detector.
  • Solution: Clean or replace the detector.

Unwanted Alarms:

  • Cause: Faulty detector or environmental factors (dust, steam).
  • Solution: Relocate detectors away from non-fire sources or replace faulty units.

Emergency Procedures

Evacuation:

  • In the event of a fire alarm, evacuate the building following designated routes.
  • Do not attempt to reset the system until the emergency has been confirmed as false or resolved.

Fire Alarm Activation:

  • Ensure the fire department or emergency services are notified immediately when the alarm is activated.

5. Safety Guidelines

Electrical and System Safety

  • Only trained and authorized personnel should operate or maintain the fire alarm system.
  • Disconnect the power supply before performing any repairs or maintenance on the control panel or detectors.
  • Use appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) when handling wiring or electrical components.

Evacuation Protocol

  • On hearing the fire alarm, all personnel should evacuate the building immediately via the nearest exit.
  • Follow designated evacuation routes and gather at pre-determined assembly points.
  • Fire wardens or safety personnel should ensure all areas are cleared, and no one remains inside.

6. Service and Spare Parts

Recommended Spare Parts

  • Smoke and heat detectors
  • Manual call points
  • Control panel fuses
  • Power supply units (including backup batteries)
  • Sounders and strobes

1. Introduction

Purpose

This manual provides comprehensive instructions for the operation, maintenance, and troubleshooting of the public address (PA) system. It is designed to ensure optimal performance, safety, and reliability of the system for day-to-day use and during emergency situations.

Overview 1

The public address (PA) system is used to make general and emergency announcements throughout a facility. It consists of microphones, amplifiers, speakers, and other devices that work together to provide clear and audible communication. The system is often zoned to allow selective paging to different areas of the building.

2. System Components

Control Unit

  • Function: The central hub for managing inputs from microphones and audio devices, routing signals to amplifiers, and controlling output to speakers.
  • Components: Power switches, volume controls, zone selectors, display panel, and audio inputs/outputs.

Microphones

Types:

  • Gooseneck Microphone: Typically used for stationary setups.
  • Handheld Microphone: For portable or mobile use.
  • Wireless Microphone: Provides flexibility of movement without cables.
  • Function: Transmits voice or audio signals to the control unit for broadcast over the PA system.

Amplifiers

  • Function: Boosts audio signals from the control unit to the appropriate power levels for speakers to distribute sound effectively.
  • Components: Input/output jacks, volume controls, and power indicators.

Speakers

Types:

  • Ceiling Speakers: Mounted in ceilings, ideal for even sound distribution in large areas.
  • Wall-Mounted Speakers: Fixed on walls for focused sound output.
  • Outdoor Speakers: Weatherproof speakers used in external areas.

Function: Convert amplified audio signals into sound for listeners.

Cabling and Connections

Types:

  • Audio Cables: Carry audio signals from the control unit to amplifiers and speakers.
  • Power Cables: Provide electrical power to amplifiers and other components.

Function: Connect various system components, enabling them to communicate and work together.

Auxiliary Devices

  • Music Source: CD player, radio, or other audio input for playing background music or pre-recorded messages.
  • Emergency Interface: Integration with fire alarm systems or other emergency protocols to automatically broadcast pre-recorded evacuation messages.

3. Operation of Public Address System

Control Unit Operation

  • Powering On:
  • Turn on the control unit by flipping the main power switch. Ensure that the amplifiers and other connected devices are also powered on.

Source Selection:

  • Select the appropriate audio source (microphone, music, pre-recorded message) from the control panel.

Microphone Use

Basic Use:

  • Press the microphone button to activate it and begin speaking. For gooseneck or handheld microphones, maintain a distance of 6-12 inches from your mouth for optimal sound clarity.
  • Speak clearly into the microphone for effective communication.

Wireless Microphone:

  • Ensure the batteries are charged and the microphone is connected to the control unit's receiver before use.

Volume and Sound Control

Adjusting Volume:

  • Use the volume controls on the control unit or amplifier to adjust sound levels to ensure clarity without distortion.
  • Adjust microphone sensitivity as needed for different speaker volumes or environments.

Sound Balance:

  • Balance the output across different zones to avoid uneven sound distribution.

Zone Selection and Paging

Zone Selection:

  • If the PA system is zoned, select the appropriate zone(s) from the control unit to broadcast messages only to specific areas of the facility.
  • All-zone paging can be used for announcements that need to be heard by the entire facility.

Paging:

  • Activate the paging function to make an announcement. Select the appropriate zone and press the “Talk” or “Page” button before speaking into the microphone.

Emergency Announcements

Pre-Recorded Messages:

  • In case of emergency, the control unit may automatically play pre-recorded evacuation messages.
  • Verify that the emergency interface is working properly with other systems such as fire alarms.

Live Announcements:

  • Authorized personnel can make live emergency announcements by selecting the all-zone option and speaking directly into the microphone.

4. Maintenance Procedures

Routine Inspection and Testing

Daily:

  • Inspect the control unit and microphones for physical damage.
  • Ensure that all power and audio connections are secure.
  • Verify that the system is functioning by making a short test announcement.

Monthly:

  • Test the system by playing audio in all zones to ensure speakers are working properly.
  • Test all microphones (wired and wireless) for clarity and volume.
  • Check the amplifier's performance by adjusting the volume and monitoring sound output.

Six Months:

  • Refer Six months Maintenance Checklist for Fire Alarm System

Annually:

  • Refer Six months Maintenance Checklist for Fire Alarm System

Troubleshooting and Fault Diagnosis

No Sound Output:

  • Cause: Power supply failure, amplifier malfunction, or broken speaker.
  • Solution: Check the power supply, reset the amplifier, and inspect speaker connections.

Distorted Sound:

  • Cause: Overloaded amplifier, poor cable connections, or faulty speaker.
  • Solution: Lower the volume, check all connections, and test each speaker for clarity.

Microphone Not Working:

  • Cause: Dead batteries (for wireless microphones), damaged cables, or control unit malfunction.
  • Solution: Replace batteries, inspect cable connections, or test the control unit.

Repairs and Component Replacement

  • Replace faulty speakers, microphones, or cables as soon as they are identified to avoid disruptions in operation.
  • Amplifiers or control units showing signs of malfunction should be serviced by a qualified technician.

5. Safety Guidelines

Electrical and System Safety

  • Ensure that the power supply to the PA system is stable and within the recommended voltage range.
  • Disconnect power before performing any repairs or maintenance to avoid electrical shock.
  • Do not overload the system by connecting too many speakers or devices to the same amplifier without checking load capacity.

Proper Use and Handling

  • Handle microphones carefully to avoid dropping or damaging them.
  • Avoid placing microphones near loudspeakers to prevent feedback loops that cause high-pitched noises.
  • Keep the control unit in a clean, dry area to prevent dust accumulation or moisture damage.8

3. Operational Procedures

3.1 System Activation

The sprinkler system is automatically activated when heat from a fire triggers one or more sprinkler heads. Once activated, water flows through the system to the affected area, suppressing the fire. In the event of system activation:

  • Alarm Activation: The flow switch will signal the alarm system, notifying building occupants and emergency responds.
  • Water Flow: Water is released through the sprinkler heads to suppress the fire.
  • Manual Operation: In case of a system malfunction or a false alarm, the sprinkler system can be manually shut off or controlled using the system's control valves.
  • Isolation of Areas: If required, specific zones of the system can be isolated using the sectional control valves to prevent water from flowing to unnecessary areas.

4. Maintenance Procedures

Regular maintenance is critical to ensure that the sprinkler system functions correctly and complies with local regulations. The following sections describe the maintenance requirements for each component.

Six Months and Annual Maintenance is provided from Nirmaan.

4.1. Routine Maintenance

  • Sprinkler Heads:
    • Check for damage or obstruction that could impede the spray pattern.
    • Ensure that sprinkler heads are properly aligned with no corrosion or buildup around the spray mechanism.
    • Replace any damaged or inactive sprinkler heads immediately.
  • Piping:
    • Inspect all exposed piping for signs of corrosion, damage, or leaks.
    • Ensure that pipes are adequately supported and free from blockages.
  • Valves:
    • Check all control valves (main, test, drain) to ensure they are fully operational.
    • Ensure that valves are not obstructed and can be easily operated during an emergency.

4.2. System Cleaning

3. Discharge Nozzles: Distribute the agent throughout the protected area.
4. Detection Sensors: Identify fire conditions and trigger the system.
5. Warning Devices: Alert personnel before discharge.

Operation Instructions

1. Power On

Ensure the control panel is connected to a reliable power source. Turn on the control panel and verify that all system components are operational.

2. System Monitoring

The control panel continuously monitors detection sensors for signs of fire. Check the status indicators on the control panel to ensure normal operation.

3. Alarm Conditions

When a fire is detected, the system will trigger an alarm. Warning devices (e.g., sirens, lights) will activate to alert personnel. Personnel should evacuate the area immediately upon hearing the alarm.

4. Gas Discharge

After the pre-programmed delay to allow evacuation, the gas will be released. Discharge nozzles will distribute the suppression agent throughout the protected area.

5. Post-Discharge Procedures

After gas discharge, ensure the area is safe before re-entry. Ventilate the area to remove any residual suppression agent. Inspect the protected area for fire damage and ensure the fire is fully extinguished.

6. System Reset

Once the area is confirmed safe, reset the control panel. Refill or replace gas cylinders as needed to restore system readiness.

Maintenance Instructions

1. Visual Checks

Inspect gas cylinders, nozzles, and detection sensors regularly. Ensure all components are free from damage and obstruction.

2. Control Panel Inspection

Verify that the control panel is functioning correctly. Check for any fault indicators or warning messages.

3. Gas Cylinder Maintenance

Check the pressure levels of gas cylinders periodically. Ensure cylinders are securely mounted and free from corrosion.

4. Detection Sensor Testing

Test detection sensors regularly to ensure they respond correctly to fire conditions. Clean sensors to remove dust and debris that may affect performance.

Troubleshooting

1. Fault Indicators

Refer to the control panel for fault codes and descriptions. Common issues include power supply problems, sensor malfunctions, and low cylinder pressure.

2. Resolving Common Issues

  • Power Issues: Ensure a stable power supply and check connections.
  • Sensor Malfunctions: Test and clean sensors; replace if necessary.
  • Low Cylinder Pressure: Refill or replace gas cylinders as needed.

Alarm Issues

1. False Alarms

Verify alarm settings and sensitivity thresholds. Check for environmental factors, such as dust or temperature fluctuations, that may cause false alarms.

2. Non-Responsive Alarms

Ensure all sensors are properly connected to the control panel. Test the alarm system and replace faulty components.

Safety Precautions

1. General Safety

Ensure all personnel are trained in the operation and emergency procedures of the gas suppression system. Follow all manufacturer guidelines and local fire safety regulations.

2. During Maintenance

Power off the system before performing any maintenance tasks. Use appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE).

3. Emergency Situations

Evacuate immediately upon hearing the alarm. Do not attempt to re-enter the area until it is confirmed safe by authorized personnel.

The gas suppression system is a critical component of your fire protection strategy, providing reliable and effective suppression of fires in enclosed areas. Regular maintenance and proper operation are essential to ensure its effectiveness. Adhere to the guidelines outlined in this manual to maintain optimal system performance and safety.

1. INTRODUCTION

The VESDA system is an advanced air-sampling smoke detection system designed to provide very early warning of fire hazards. It operates by continuously drawing air from the protected area through a network of sampling pipes and analyzing it for the presence of smoke particles using high-sensitivity laser detection technology.

The system typically consists of:

  • Detection Unit (VESDA detector)
  • Air Sampling Pipe Network
  • Filters and Aspirator (fan)
  • Display/Control Panel

2. SYSTEM OPERATION

2.1 System Start-Up

  • Ensure all electrical connections are secure and power supply is available.
  • Switch ON the main power supply to the VESDA unit.
  • Allow the system to initialize and complete self-diagnostics.
  • Verify that the display panel indicates normal operating status.
  • Check airflow levels and ensure no fault indications are present.

2.2 Normal Operation

  • The system continuously samples air through the pipe network.
  • The detector analyzes air using a laser chamber to detect smoke particles.
  • Smoke levels are displayed in real-time on the control panel.
  • The system operates with multiple alarm thresholds:
    • Alert Level
    • Action Level
    • Fire 1
    • Fire 2

2.3 Alarm Conditions and Response

Alert Level

  • Indicates very low smoke presence.
  • Action: Investigate area for early signs of smoke.

Action Level

  • Indicates increased smoke concentration.
  • Action: Perform detailed inspection and prepare for emergency response.

Fire 1 / Fire 2

  • Indicates confirmed fire condition.
  • Action:
    • Activate emergency procedures.
    • Notify fire response team.
    • Initiate evacuation if required.
  • If a false alarm is suspected:
    • Identify the cause (dust, contamination, etc.)
    • Rectify the issue
    • Reset the system via the control panel

2.4 System Reset

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 Purpose of This Manual

This Operations & Maintenance (O&M) Manual provides comprehensive guidelines for the safe operation, routine inspection, testing, troubleshooting, and maintenance of the Water Leak Detection (WLD) System installed in the facility. The objective of the WLD system is to detect the presence of water leakage at an early stage and generate audible, visual and system alarms to prevent damage to critical equipment, finishes, and building infrastructure.

1.2 Scope of the System

The WLD system covered under this manual includes the following major components:

  • Water Leak Detection (WLD) Control Panel
  • Sensor Cable (Leak Detection Cable)
  • Point Sensors (if applicable)
  • Audio-Visual Alarm Devices (WLD Hooter, Beacon)
  • Interconnecting Cables & Accessories
  • Interface with BMS / EMS (where applicable)

This manual applies to all areas protected by the WLD system such as:

  • Data centers and server rooms
  • Electrical switch rooms
  • Battery rooms
  • HVAC plant rooms
  • Toilets, pantries, and wet areas (as applicable)
  • Under raised floors and above false ceilings

2. SYSTEM OVERVIEW

2.1 Working Principle

The Water Leak Detection System continuously monitors designated areas using sensor cables or point sensors. When water comes into contact with the sensing elements, a change in electrical resistance is detected. This change is processed by the WLD control panel, which then:

  • Identifies the presence of water leakage
  • Locates the approximate leak position (for distance-measuring systems)
  • Activates audible and visual alarms
  • Sends alarm signals to BMS/SCADA systems (if interfaced)

2.2 System Architecture

The typical WLD system architecture consists of:

  • Sensor cable laid along potential leakage paths
  • Sensor cable connected to zone inputs of WLD panel
  • WLD panel powered through UPS-backed power supply
  • Alarm outputs connected to hooter and beacon
  • Communication outputs connected to BMS or monitoring system

3. EQUIPMENT DESCRIPTION

3.1 Water Leak Detection (WLD) Control Panel

3.1.1 Description

The WLD control panel is the central monitoring and control unit of the system. It continuously supervises the sensor cables, processes alarm signals, displays system status, and activates output devices.

3.1.2 Main Features

  • Multi-zone or addressable monitoring
  • LCD / LED display for system status
  • Visual indicators for Normal, Alarm, Fault, and Power status
  • Alarm acknowledgment and reset functions
  • Relay outputs for alarm, fault, and system status
  • RS-485 / TCP-IP / Modbus / BACnet interface (model dependent)

3.1.3 Panel Indications

  • Power ON: Indicates normal power supply
  • Normal: System healthy, no leak detected
  • Leak Alarm: Water detected in a monitored zone
  • Cable Fault / Open / Short: Sensor cable integrity issue
  • Communication Fault: BMS communication failure

3.2 Sensor Cable

3.2.1 Description

Sensor cable is a water-sensitive cable designed to detect the presence of moisture along its entire length. It is installed along floors, near pipelines, under raised floors, or below equipment prone to leakage.

3.2.2 Construction

  • Two or more sensing conductors
  • Insulated carrier wires
  • Outer protective jacket (as per application)

3.2.3 Installation Guidelines

  • Laid directly on floor or mounted using clips
  • Avoid sharp bends and crushing
  • Minimum bending radius as per manufacturer
  • Cable joints to be avoided wherever possible
  • Keep away from power cables to avoid interference

3.3 Point Sensors (If Applicable)

Point sensors are discrete leak detectors used at specific locations such as under AHUs, pumps, or water tanks. These sensors trigger an alarm when water bridges the sensing electrodes.

3.4 WLD Hooter / Audible Alarm

3.4.1 Description

The WLD hooter provides an audible alert during a leak or fault condition to ensure immediate attention by operations staff.

3.4.2 Operating Conditions

  • Operates on panel output voltage (typically 24V DC)
  • Activated automatically during alarm condition
  • Can be silenced through panel acknowledgment

3.5 Visual Alarm (Beacon / Lamp)

Visual indicators provide a flashing signal to supplement audible alarms, especially in noisy areas.

4. OPERATING INSTRUCTIONS

4.1 Normal Operation

  • Ensure WLD panel power supply is ON
  • System should indicate NORMAL status
  • No audible alarm or fault indication should be active
  • Periodically check panel display for system health

4.2 Alarm Condition (Leak Detected)

When water leakage occurs:

  • Sensor cable detects moisture
  • WLD panel registers leak alarm
  • Alarm LED turns ON
  • Hooter activates
  • Leak location / zone displayed on panel
  • Alarm signal transmitted to BMS (if connected)

Operator Action:

  • Acknowledge alarm on panel
  • Identify affected zone/location
  • Inspect site physically and stop water source
  • Dry the sensor cable thoroughly
  • Reset system after rectification

4.3 Fault Condition

Fault conditions may include

  • Sensor cable open or short
  • Power supply failure
  • Communication failure

Operator Action:

  • Note fault indication
  • Inspect wiring and sensor cable
  • Rectify issue
  • Reset panel

4.4 Alarm Acknowledgment & Reset

  • Acknowledge: Silences hooter but alarm remains active
  • Reset: Clears alarm after leak is rectified and sensor cable is dry

5. MAINTENANCE PROCEDURES

5.1 Routine Maintenance Schedule

ActivityFrequency
Visual inspection of panelWeekly
Sensor cable inspectionMonthly
Functional alarm testingQuarterly
BMS signal verificationQuarterly
Full system testingAnnually

5.2 Sensor Cable Inspection

  • Check for physical damage
  • Ensure cable is clean and dry
  • Verify cable routing is intact
  • Ensure cable clips are secure

5.3 Functional Testing Procedure

  • Pour a small quantity of clean water on sensor cable
  • Verify alarm activation on panel
  • Confirm hooter and beacon operation
  • Verify BMS alarm receipt
  • Dry sensor cable using cloth or air blower
  • Reset system

5.4 Panel Maintenance

  • Keep panel clean and dust-free
  • Check terminal tightness annually
  • Verify power supply voltage
  • Ensure backup power availability

6. TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE

IssuePossible CauseCorrective Action
No power indicationPower supply failureCheck MCB, SMPS, UPS supply
False alarmsMoisture, condensationDry sensor cable, improve insulation
Cable fault alarmDamaged cableRepair or replace cable section
No hooter soundHooter wiring faultCheck wiring and output relay
No BMS signalCommunication faultCheck protocol and cabling

7. SAFETY PRECAUTIONS

  • Always isolate power before maintenance
  • Do not immerse sensor cable permanently in water
  • Avoid chemical exposure unless cable is rated
  • Follow electrical safety procedures

1.1 Purpose of This Manual

This Operations & Maintenance (O&M) Manual provides detailed guidelines for the safe operation, routine inspection, testing, troubleshooting and maintenance of the Rodent Repellent (RR) System installed in the facility. The primary purpose of the system is to prevent rodent infestation by generating ultrasonic / electromagnetic signals that deter rodents from protected areas without causing harm to humans or equipment.

1.2 Scope of the System

This manual covers the following major components of the Rodent Repellent System:

  • Rodent Repellent (RR) Control Panel
  • Ultrasonic / Electromagnetic Transducers
  • Zone Control Modules (if applicable)
  • Power Supply Units
  • Interconnecting Cables & Accessories
  • Interface with BMS / EMS (if applicable)Rodent Repellent (RR) Control Panel
  • Ultrasonic / Electromagnetic Transducers
  • Zone Control Modules (if applicable)
  • Power Supply Units
  • Interconnecting Cables & Accessories
  • Interface with BMS / EMS (if applicable)

The system is typically installed in:

  • Electrical switch rooms and panels
  • Server rooms and data centers
  • UPS rooms and battery rooms
  • HVAC plant rooms
  • Cable basements, shafts and trenches
  • False floor and false ceiling areas

2. SYSTEM OVERVIEW

2.1 Working Principle

The Rodent Repellent System works by emitting high-frequency ultrasonic sound waves and/or electromagnetic pulses through connected transducers.

These signals create an uncomfortable environment for rodents, affecting their nervous system and communication, thereby forcing them to vacate the protected area.

The system operates continuously or in programmed cycles to ensure uninterrupted protection.

2.2 System Architecture

The typical RR system consists of:

  • Central RR control panel with multiple zone outputs
  • Ultrasonic / electromagnetic transducers installed in protected areas
  • Power supply through UPS-backed electrical source
  • Alarm and fault outputs for monitoring
  • Optional BMS interface for status and alarms

3. EQUIPMENT DESCRIPTION

3.1 Rodent Repellent (RR) Control Panel

3.1.1 Description

The RR control panel is the central unit that generates and distributes ultrasonic or electromagnetic signals to the connected transducers. It monitors system health, power status and output continuity.

3.1.2 Main Features

  • Multi-zone output capability
  • Adjustable frequency and intensity levels
  • LED / LCD indicators for system status
  • Individual zone ON/OFF control
  • Fault detection for transducer or wiring failure
  • Alarm relay outputs for system fault
  • BMS interface via dry contact / RS-485 (model dependent)

3.1.3 Panel Indications

  • Power ON: Normal power supply available
  • System Active: Ultrasonic signal generation healthy
  • Zone Active: Corresponding zone operational
  • Fault: Transducer / wiring / internal fault

3.2 Ultrasonic / Electromagnetic Transducers

3.2.1 Description

Transducers are field devices that emit ultrasonic sound waves or electromagnetic pulses generated by the RR panel. They are strategically placed to ensure full area coverage

3.2.2 Technical Characteristics

  • Operating frequency typically above 20 kHz
  • Non-audible to humans
  • Continuous or pulsed output
  • Low power consumption
  • Designed for indoor industrial environments

3.2.3 Installation Guidelines

  • Mounted at recommended height (typically 300–600 mm from floor)
  • Clear line of sight to protected area
  • Avoid obstruction by heavy equipment
  • Maintain spacing as per manufacturer recommendations
  • Avoid installation near sensitive audio equipment

3.3 Zone Control Modules (If Applicable)

Zone modules allow independent control, monitoring, and isolation of specific areas. Each zone can be tested or isolated without affecting other zones.

3.4 Power Supply Unit

The system is powered through a regulated SMPS, typically 230V AC to low-voltage DC, backed by UPS where required to ensure continuous operation during power failure.

4. OPERATING INSTRUCTIONS

4.1 Normal Operation

  • Ensure RR panel power supply is ON
  • Verify all zone indicators show ACTIVE status
  • No fault or alarm indication should be present
  • System operates continuously without operator intervention

4.2 Start-Up Procedure

  • Switch ON incoming power supply
  • Verify panel self-test completion
  • Confirm system active indication
  • Verify all transducers are operational

4.3 Shutdown Procedure (If Required)

  • Inform concerned stakeholders
  • Switch OFF zone outputs (if required)
  • Switch OFF main power supply

Note: Shutdown should be avoided unless maintenance is required, as continuous operation ensures effectiveness.

4.4 Fault Condition Handling

Possible fault conditions include:

  • Transducer open / short circuit
  • Power supply failure
  • Internal panel fault

Operator Action:

  • Identify fault indication on panel
  • Isolate affected zone
  • Inspect wiring and transducers
  • Rectify fault and reset system

5. MAINTENANCE PROCEDURES

5.1 Routine Maintenance Schedule

ActivityFrequency
Panel visual inspectionWeekly
Transducer inspectionMonthly
Zone functional testingQuarterly
Wiring & terminal checkHalf-yearly
Complete system auditAnnually

5.2 Transducer Inspection

  • Check physical condition and mounting
  • Ensure no dust accumulation or obstruction
  • Verify output using panel test mode
  • Replace damaged or non-functional units

5.3 Functional Testing Procedure

  • Activate test mode from RR panel
  • Verify zone-wise transducer operation
  • Confirm fault indication when a transducer is isolated
  • Restore normal operation
  • Record test results

5.4 Panel Maintenance

  • Clean panel using dry cloth
  • Check SMPS output voltage
  • Tighten terminals annually
  • Verify relay outputs and BMS signals

6.TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE

IssuePossible CauseCorrective Action
System not powering ONPower supply failureCheck MCB, SMPS, UPS
Zone inactiveTransducer or wiring faultInspect and replace faulty device
Frequent faultsLoose connectionsTighten terminals
No BMS statusCommunication issueCheck cabling and protocol
Reduced effectivenessImproper placementReposition transducers

7. SAFETY PRECAUTIONS

  • Isolate power before maintenance
  • Do not modify frequency beyond recommended limits
  • Ensure compliance with local electrical safety standards
  • Avoid prolonged exposure during testing near transducers
